en: [C160/00-1; B66b-5] Thus, when Makaranda has set out for Mādhava’s presence taking Madayantikā with him, there is the entrance of Avalokitā to introduce the events concerning Mādhava, who has departed taking Mālatī and is staying in the vicinity of Kāmandakī’s convent. AVALOKITĀ: I have paid my respects to the Venerable Lady upon her return from Nandana’s residence. Therefore, I shall now go to Mālatī and Mādhava. Here they are, adorning the stone slab on the bank of the long pond, having just finished their bath at the end of the summer day.
[Mādhava] [1] *Udyan*: rising upward. Here the simile is that the *ketakī* pollen is like a cloud moving upward in the sky with the force of the wind.
[1] *Upāvartaye*: I cause to turn toward me. The meaning is: "I inspire such confidence in her that she resorts to a relaxed posture."

The words *yāvat* and *tāvat* refer here to the duration and extent of the embrace. The address *sutanu* (O slender-limbed one) is appropriate for the request of an embrace that involves the entire body. *Sāndratā* (density) results from its continuous extension; *pratanutā* (thinness) results from having attained an excellence of subtlety.

The drops of water falling from the mass of hair serve to soothe the heat of the summer; the moist state between the bud-like breasts produces a coolness that brings about a numbness pervading the entire body upon the emergence of horripilation. *Aṅkapālīm*: merely an embrace.
*Ayī* expresses feigned anger.

*Samūḍhaḥ*: well-held. *Cumbanam*: contact. *Vibhramaḥ*: confusion. "May you place upon my neck an arm resembling a necklace of moonstones, which has the nature of oozing at the touch of moonbeams—an arm from which drops of perspiration have appeared due to the force of your well-maintained agitation. A necklace too, by its coolness, is offered to the neck to restore life. By saying "this," he expresses his own unworthiness while manifesting the other's favor. By saying "by you," he incites the heroine.

[4] *Nirvāpitam* means rendered free from heat (*nistāpaṃ kṛtam*). The address “O you with the voice of a *kiṃnara*” is intended to nourish the sweetness of her speech. In the first half of the verse, the word *tu* has the sense of *yadi* (if), while the second has the sense of *punar* (but). The underlying meaning is: "If embracing and such are deemed improper, then let this person be cooled by the downpour of the sweet essence of your conversation. By stating that even the sweet song of the cuckoo becomes harsh to the hollows of her ears when you speak, she reveals her own state of passionate attachment. [4]

Avalokitā: O you who are habitually unable to finish what you have begun! That you, now feeling distressed because Mādhava has been out of sight for even a moment, say before me, "The noble son is delaying; I wonder after how long I shall see him, so that, having cast off all timidity and looking upon him with my blinking forgotten as an obstacle, I might say, 'May he honor me with a double-twisted embrace'?"—this is now the result. The word *yad idānīm* is used as a rhetorical ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*). The word *sāṃpratam* is used here with a gesture of shaking the head.
Envy (*asūyā*) is the revelation of faults in the midst of virtues; it is characterized by envy because it involves the disclosure of secrets.
Mādhava asks: "My dear, is this true?
A nod of the head serves to negate what has been said.
[Mādhava] (3) *Anavasitaḥ*: one who has not reached a certainty.

[5] That cheek upon which, while being washed with a mouthful of water, the moon shines as if it had placed its ray-like lotus stalks there to drink the nectar of beauty—how is it that this very cheek is now being washed? [5] Avalokitā: Friend, why is she weeping now with such a gushing flood of tears?
*Ucchalitaḥ*: becoming abundant; *bāṣpasya*: of tears; *utpīḍaḥ*: the emergence as they gather into a mass—having acted in such a way.

Mālatī: Friend, how much longer must I endure the sorrow of my dear friend’s absence? (4) Even news of her is difficult to obtain. Avalokitā: It is precisely through your conversation that she remembers Lavaṅgikā and grows anxious for news of her.
"It is yours alone," [she said], because Mādhava had declared, "I adjure you by the lives of both Lavaṅgikā and Avalokitā.

AVALOKITĀ: Noble sir, since you were first commissioned by the venerable lady—who was announcing the festival of the cessation of Makaranda’s swoon, which was adorned by the claws of a tiger—to offer your heart along with your life to Mālatī, what reward will there be now for anyone who congratulates you this very moment upon the attainment of Madayantī?

The phrase "proclaiming the festival of the cessation of delusion" (*mohavirāmotsavaṃ nivedayantyā*) is construed in grammatical apposition with "by Mālatī" (*mālatyā*). The expression "along with life" (*saha jīvitenā*) is clear from the verse beginning with "wounded by the serpent" (*yad vyālavraṇita°*). (5) [Mādhava:
*Anuyoga* means a question. The observation of Mālatī’s heart is for the purpose of contemplating the first half of the upcoming verse. *Kesarā* means the *vakula* tree. *Prasava* means a flower.

[6] That garland which was brought by my dear friend Lavaṅgikā—thinking it had been woven by me herself—was placed with affection upon the expanse of her breast. Then, when the time for her marriage to Nandana arrived, although she had lost all hope regarding me, she surrendered it as if it were her very life out of the delusion that it was Lavaṅgikā. Thus, by reminding her of this former history of passion, the heroine is inspired with confidence. *Vistārī* means expansive or broad.
By the word *kumbha*, height is indicated; by the word *kuṭmala*, softness; and by the word *bhara*, fullness. *Dāya* is that which is given. [6]
Avalokitā: Friend Mālatī, this *vakula* garland is indeed dear to you; therefore, be attentive. (6) For now it will suddenly fall into the hands of another.

If Makaranda’s touching of Madayantikā were to be described by someone else, then it would belong to that speaker; however, since this [act] is extremely dear to you, you should speak of it and take [the reward]—with this reasoning, Saudāmanī should bring about the arrangement for joining Mālatī’s necklace to her neck in the ninth act, as a means of conversation between Mālatī and Mādhava and as a token of recognition for Mālatī. MĀLATĪ: My dear friend, she gives me good advice.
Avalokitā: "O friend, please instruct me; you yourself tell me [the way], so that I may speak"—this is the meaning.
(7) AVALOKITĀ: Like the sound of footsteps.
MĀLATĪ: By good fortune, you are prospering through the recovery of Madayantikā!

[Mādhava: Once again, there is the attainment of sharing in pleasant conversation. Avalokitā: Indeed, the burden of the venerable lady’s expectations has been fulfilled by Buddharakṣitā. Mālatī: We see our dear friend Lavaṅgikā.
Lavaṅgikā: Let the noble sir protect us! Indeed, midway along the road, Makaranda was attacked by the city guards; we have been sent here by Kalahaṃsaka, who met us at that moment.
*Abhiyoga* means an assault.
Kalahaṃsaka: From the way the clamor of battle has been heard by those coming toward us from this direction, I infer that another hostile force has also arrived.

*Āyodhana*: battle. *Pārakyaṃ balaṃ*—this is a regional (deśī) expression for "the enemy's force. *Mālatyavalokite*: joy and agitation have arrived simultaneously for the enjoyment [of both]. [Mādhava: [7] Regarding "of Hari": for the lion who desires to manifest boundless valor, his own paw alone is a companion to his majesty. Of what nature is it? He is that sole hero in the shattering of the bone situated upon the head of that lordly elephant, whose face has been drenched by the rut-fluid falling from the cavity of its split-open frontal globe. [7]
The Immediate Successor: the second.
Avalokitā, Lavāṅgikā, and Buddharakṣitā: "May these noble ones indeed return unharmed.

Mālatī: Friends Buddharakṣitā and Avalokitā, go quickly and report this news to the Blessed Lady. And you, dear friend Lavāṅgikā, inform the Noble Son with the utmost haste: "If we are still worthy of your compassion, then proceed with vigilance."

Mālatī: Alas! It is not known how so much time has passed. Very well; I shall remain here, watching the path by which my dear friend Lavaṅgikā returns. (8) Here, "gamyatām" means "let her be led away" by way of departure. (9) "Pratinivṛttiḥ" means returning after having turned back.
Madayantikā: My left eye is throbbing.

*Vāma* means unfavorable; *avāma* means right (or favorable). And for women, a throbbing on the right side is unfavorable. This indicates the entrance of Kapālakuṇḍalā. At this moment, having dispatched Buddharakṣitā and Avalokitā to Kāmandakī and Lavaṅgikā to Mādhava, Mālatī has left Madayantikā’s side and, out of excessive haste, has moved ahead alone. MĀLATĪ: Alas, noble son!
[KAPĀLAKUṆḌALĀ]: Wailing; shrieking.

[8] The Libertine: A great lover; that is to say, one whose passion is manifest. The Falcon: One with outstretched palms; its "descent" (*avapāta*) is the swooping down from the sky with excessive speed. (10) The Quail: The female of a particular bird well-known as *vadvahi*. And she is "young," meaning a girl, and thus, due to her extreme delicacy, she is unable to endure mistreatment. [8] MADAYANTIKĀ: I too shall follow Mālatī alone. (11) Friend Mālatī. LAVAṄGIKĀ: I am indeed Lavaṅgikā.
MADAYANTIKĀ: Have you seen the noble one? The word *api* is used here as an interrogative particle. *Saṃbhāvitaḥ* means "found" or, in other words, "discovered."

Lavaṅgikā: Friend, as soon as he emerged from the garden enclosure, he heard the tumultuous noise; with a violent, forceful rush of his massive thighs, he charged and entered the enemy ranks. (12) Since then, I, unfortunate as I am, have returned. And in every house I hear the lamentations of the citizens, who are overflowing with affection for his virtues: "O noble Mādhava! O Makaranda! O reckless one!"

It is said that the Great King, having heard the account of the deception regarding the two ministers' daughters, was seized by a surge of indignation; at that very moment, he dismissed his troop of foot soldiers and, standing upon the roof-terrace of the palace in the moonlight, watched—so it is reported.

*Udyānavāṭaḥ*: a garden path; its *upanirgamaḥ*: a small path nearby. *Avakṣepaḥ*: disregard. *Apaviddham*—meaning *apakṣiptam* (cast aside)—is an indication of a sickle. *Vikaṭam*: vast. *Dhūā*: daughter. *Vipralambhaḥ*: deception. *Candrātapaḥ*: moonlight. This expression is used because, during the state of Malati’s suffering from separation, that [moonlight] was habitually treated as an *uddīpanavibhāva* (an excitant cause). "It is being discussed"—that is, by the citizens themselves. *Madayantikā*: "Alas! I am destroyed, I of little fortune."
Lāvaṅgikā: Friend, where is Mālatī now?
Madayantikā: Friend, she indeed set out first to look for your path, and I followed after. But I do not see her. She might have disappeared into the thicket of the garden.
*Prasṛtā*: gone forth. *Sā nāma*: "She, perhaps"—this expresses a doubt. *Pranaṣṭā*: one whose path has been lost.
Lavaṅgikā: Friend, let us search quickly. My dear friend is extremely distressed; at this moment, she cannot sustain her life while staying in the grove.
Both: Friend Mālatī! Indeed, I am saying, "Friend Mālatī!
(13) Kalahaṃsaka: By good fortune, I have emerged safely from that difficult and perilous encounter.
"Hīmāṇahe" is used by a person of low status to express wonder and satisfaction, just like saying "O mother! O mother! in distress.

I seem to behold a host of others, terrifying to look upon and radiant with the rays of the moon reflected in streams of water from polished swords brandished incessantly and without stain; their mass resembles the swollen, agitated current of the daughter of Kalinda (the Yamunā) as it is effortlessly spread upward by the plow wielded with playful ease by the mighty arms of Kāmapāla in his intoxicated sport; and it resounds with a clamor that fills the entire expanse of the courtyard of the sky, arising from the frantic retreats of rival warriors who are distressed by the merciless and violent agitation caused by Makaranda’s unrestrained leaps. (14)

*Pārakkaaṃ*: the enemy's force (*parakīyabala*); the connection is that [the poet] says, "I seem to see its multitude even now. By nature stainless, constantly brandished (*uddhūta*), meaning shaken, and polished (*dhauta*), meaning refined by the smith—those *taravārayaḥ*, i.e., swords; with the moonbeams reflected upon their edges, it is such that its appearance is both radiant (*ujjvala*)—meaning beautiful—and terrifying (*viḍurilla*).

By the broad staff-like arms of Balabhadra, who had been embraced by Madalīlā, the stream of the Yamunā was tossed—that is, driven in a curved motion—by the play of the plow (or, according to another reading, by the furrow made by the plow); it was thus expanded (*virillida*) and surging upward (*uvvellira*). Equal in width to that [stream], the torrent fell headlong and from above in an unrestrained manner, taking many forms, as did the fierce and merciless *makaranda* [nectar].

I remember my lord Mādhava, who performed a perilous feat of daring by traversing paths cleared of all enemies—paths from which every hostile army had been swiftly driven away after their weapons were snatched from the hands of brave warriors by the cage-like impact of his terrifying thunderbolt-arms, shattering their frames. Furthermore, I recall the tumultuous clamor that spread across the entire expanse of the sky due to the flight of his adversaries, who were overwhelmed by his fierce agitation and turned back in retreat.

"I remember Mādhava"—this is the connection [of the sentence]. Because his cage-like body was shattered by the thunderbolt of his terrifying arms, those brave warriors who had fled—meaning, those who had made an effort to escape—had various weapons snatched away and seized from their hands. By that very army of enemies which had been struck down with those [weapons], a formidable and swift retreat—that is, a flight—was initiated; by means of that, he was separated [from them].
The path is empty; therein, through his movement, he brought to an end the violent and reckless acts. (15) Likewise,

Oh, how the king’s affection for virtue has been stirred! For now, having had his agitation calmed by the humble entreaties of the doorkeeper who descended from the palace roof, he repeatedly extends his moist eyes toward the moon-like faces of Mādhava and Makaranda; and having learned their lineage from Kalahaṃsaka, he has bestowed upon them a most precious and profound honor. As for Bhūrivasu and Nandana, whose faces are stained with the soot of trembling pride, jealousy, and embarrassment, what will he say to you two now with his sweet words?

"Having awakened [the King] with the thought, 'There is no lack of satisfaction regarding my two sons-in-law—who are ornaments to the expanse of the world, possessed of great majesty, and delightful due to their virtues as new sights,' the King has gone inside. (16) "Since these two, Mādhava and Makaranda, have also arrived, I too shall inform the Blessed Lady of this news."

Having descended from the palace roof and observed the true forms of Mādhava and Makaranda, the doorkeeper led Kalahaṃsaka into the presence of the king. "Ummaccha" means jealousy; and that belongs to Nandana. When the embarrassment caused by envy was removed from Bhūrivasu, it remained as the reality belonging to Nandana.
[Makaranda: "Nirvyāja" means natural; "ūrjita" means powerful.

[9] "Crushing with the arms" (*dorniṣpeṣa*): crushing (*niṣpeṣa*) means pulverizing with the two arms (*dor-bhyām*). By that means, the masses were shattered; their compact formations fell apart, and as the skeletons were being torn asunder and split open, they overwhelmed the heroes. Immediately thereafter, having snatched away their weapons and displaying great prowess, the path ahead became terrifying, lined with rows of foot soldiers whose feet were pinned down by the pair of directions—left and right—as they strode forward. They surged upward (*udvellanti*).
Because they are still alive, they quiver; the path of this ocean-like battle—which is filled with multitudes of their headless, trunkless body fragments that lie close together—is [the path].

[9] [MĀDHAVA: [10] "Bestowing playful embraces" is an epithet for the honey (*madhu*). For when the beloveds have drunk the honey remaining from their lover’s mouthfuls, they joyfully embrace their lovers. "Insubstantial" means trivial; "distraught" means impaired. The meaning is that their charming gestures, seen and lost in an instant, are under the sway of past karma. The comparison to a bolt (*argala*) is intended to suggest its length. [10]

[11] This is the speech of Mālatī’s friend. That is Madayantikā; when she recounts the incident of the battle to you, because that incident was rooted in the audacity undertaken by Madayantikā, Mālatī—being struck by smiling side-long glances—will, with a blossoming sense of bashfulness, lower her lotus-face with a steady gaze.
[11] LAVANGIKĀ and MADAYANTIKĀ: Friend Mālatī! By good fortune, those two noble ones are seen again, unhurt.
UBHE: Whence is Mālatī here? We two unfortunate ones have been deceived by the sound of footsteps. The meaning is that she said to us, "Friend Mālatī.
[MĀDHAVA: "How? expresses astonishment. "In some way" means in an indescribable manner. "It is shattered": it finds no stability in one place.

[12] *Anubaddhaḥ*: "Pursued," meaning "interwoven" (*anusyūta*), that in which there is a trembling. And this is a painful statement regarding you two here. It is "painful" (*kaṣṭa*) because it causes distress. "In every way" (*sarvathā*) refers to the unanimity between the inner self, the bird, and the speech-form consisting of the observed collection of circumstances. [12]

MADAYANTIKĀ: At that time, indeed, when the noble lady had departed from here, I sent Lavaṅgikā after her with the message: "Having dismissed Buddharakṣitā and Avalokitā to the presence of the Blessed Lady, inform the Noble Son [Makaranda] regarding the matter of vigilance. Anxious to see her path, she set out ahead while I followed behind. I did not see her. Then we searched through the spaces between the branches until you were seen.

[Mādhava: [13] Something other than auspicious things; that is to say, something undesirable. And the address "O fierce one" (*caṇḍi*) is used out of affectionate anger. Now, if you perceive me in this manner—that is, if you wish to test me—then I am perceived. Therefore, speak! "Wanders": she finds no place of rest. "Agitated": lacking composure. [13] BOTH: Alas, dear friend, where have you gone?

[Mādhava: "And you too. This is a reminder of the sequence of the secret marriage; the sense is: "Do you not know those actions he intends to undertake out of timidity? By this, the implication is: "I am distressed, fearing that she might perhaps resolve upon some great misfortune.
Both: "This too is possible."

[Makaranda: [14] The happiness derived from the reunion of relatives, friends, and those who are objects of affection is as fleeting as a flash of lightning, for it is seen and lost in an instant; thus, there is a sense of detachment (*vairāgya*) toward cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), and this indicates the imminent entrance of a new character. She is indeed the disciple of Kāmandakī named Saudāmanī. Through her manifestation—specifically through her bringing of the *vakula* garland—the happiness is merely "unsteady" (*cañcala*), that is, it is in a state of constant flux; the meaning is that its appearance has only just begun. It is indicated that she will bring about true happiness. [14] All is well.
The Eighth Act.
